subject: history
displayName: KS3 History — Interpretations, Significance & Historical Arguments
subtitle: Why historians disagree, how significance is judged, and how to construct historical arguments.

data.targetWord: an explanation or view of the past, usually based on evidence, that answers questions such as why something happened or how significant it was

examples.en-GB: One historian argued that the Norman Conquest mainly mattered because it changed who owned land in England.

data.targetWord: something from the time being studied, or connected to it, that historians use as evidence — such as a law, letter, object, diary, building, map or painting

examples.en-GB: A medieval tax record is a source because it comes from the period being studied.

data.targetWord: a supported answer to a historical question, including a clear point, accurate evidence, explanation, and a reasoned judgement

examples.en-GB: The printing press was significant because it allowed ideas to spread much more quickly across Europe.

data.targetWord: a reasoned decision about what is most convincing or important, made after considering the evidence

examples.en-GB: Overall, the long-term impact was more significant than the immediate impact.

data.targetWord: historical importance — how much something mattered at the time, how many people it affected, how long-lasting its impact was, and whether it became a symbol for later generations

examples.en-GB: The Industrial Revolution was significant because it changed work, cities and technology across Britain.

data.targetWord: the standards used to make a judgement — in history these include the number of people affected, long-term impact, importance at the time, and symbolic importance

examples.en-GB: Using significance criteria, a historian might judge that the Black Death was very significant because it affected millions of people.

data.targetWord: information about where a source comes from — who made it, when, why, and for whom — which helps historians judge how useful and reliable it is

examples.en-GB: A speech made by a king may have a different purpose from a private diary, so provenance matters.

data.targetWord: the reason a source or interpretation was created — for example to persuade, inform, entertain, record, or criticise

examples.en-GB: A TV programme's purpose is often to entertain, which may cause it to simplify complex historical events.

data.targetWord: the people a source or interpretation was intended for, which can shape what is included, how it is written, and how complex it is

examples.en-GB: A KS3 textbook is written for a different audience than an academic history journal.

data.targetWord: the wider situation at the time a source was made, which can explain why it says what it does

examples.en-GB: A source written during wartime may show fear, patriotism or the effects of censorship.

data.targetWord: the later effects or memory of something — how an event or person continued to matter to future generations

examples.en-GB: Roman roads influenced later transport routes, showing the legacy of Roman engineering in Britain.

data.targetWord: a reason, cause, or part of an explanation for why something happened — historians often compare multiple factors

examples.en-GB: Money, religion, leadership and technology are all factors that historians might use to explain the English Civil War.

data.targetWord: specific information used to support a historical point, making an argument more convincing and precise

examples.en-GB: The evidence that some labourers demanded higher wages suggests labour shortages gave workers more bargaining power.

data.targetWord: a historical answer that considers more than one side of an argument before reaching a final judgement

examples.en-GB: A balanced answer about the Industrial Revolution would consider both the new jobs it created and the dangerous working conditions.

data.targetWord: the final reasoned judgement at the end of a historical answer, stating which argument is most convincing and why

examples.en-GB: Therefore, I think the most significant factor was political pressure because Parliament had to pass the law.

data.targetWord: effects that continued to matter years or centuries after an event — one of the key criteria for judging historical significance

examples.en-GB: Magna Carta's long-term impact was that later generations used it as a symbol of limits on royal power.

data.targetWord: when an event or document becomes a powerful symbol for later people, representing ideas or values beyond its original context

examples.en-GB: Magna Carta gained symbolic importance because later generations used it to argue for limits on rulers.

data.targetWord: a paragraph structure for history answers: Point, Evidence, Explain, Link — each part builds towards a supported historical argument

examples.en-GB: Using PEEL, a student makes a clear point, adds evidence, explains how it supports the point, then links back to the question.

data.targetWord: working out something that a source implies but does not state directly, by reading between the lines using the content and context

examples.en-GB: From a record saying fields were not harvested, a historian can infer there was a labour shortage.

data.targetWord: an event or development that brought about major change in direction, so that things were significantly different afterwards

examples.en-GB: Historians debate whether 1066 was a turning point because some Anglo-Saxon systems continued under the Normans.

data.targetWord: the historical concept of identifying what became different over time (change) alongside what stayed the same (continuity) — good answers address both

examples.en-GB: After the Black Death, some things changed (higher wages for some workers) while others continued (landlords still tried to control labour).

data.targetWord: the ordering of events in time, and understanding what came before, during and after an event — including whether change was quick or gradual

examples.en-GB: Good chronology about Magna Carta means knowing it came before Parliament and understanding the slow development between them.

data.targetWord: how deeply an event changed people's lives — whether it affected their work, rights, beliefs, wealth, power, or everyday experiences

examples.en-GB: The Black Death had great depth of impact because it changed labour relations, wages and the power balance between peasants and lords.

data.targetWord: a historical answer that only presents one viewpoint without considering alternative evidence or arguments — usually weaker than a balanced answer

examples.en-GB: Saying only that the Industrial Revolution improved Britain ignores the dangerous conditions and long hours faced by factory workers.

data.targetWord: what a source does not tell us — gaps, missing viewpoints, or ways in which the source's purpose or provenance make it incomplete as evidence

examples.en-GB: A source written by a factory owner has limitations because it may not reflect the experiences of factory workers.

To judge ____, historians use criteria such as the number of people affected, long-term impact, and symbolic importance.
Information about who made a source, when, why, and for whom is called ____.
A historical ____ includes a clear point, accurate evidence, explanation, and a reasoned judgement.
In PEEL, the letters stand for Point, Evidence, Explain, and ____.
When an event becomes a powerful symbol for later generations, historians describe its ____.
The word ____ is used to introduce a contrast or alternative view in a historical argument.
The word ____ is used to show a consequence or final judgement in a historical argument.
Working out what a source implies without stating it directly is called making an ____.
The later effects or memory of an event — how it continued to matter to future generations — is called its ____.
Interpretations can differ because historians may ask different questions, use different ____, or focus on different groups.
An answer that only presents one viewpoint without considering alternatives is called a ____ answer.
A modern history textbook about Roman Britain is an ____ of that period, not a primary source from it.
The word ____ gives a reason in a historical sentence, linking a fact to its significance.
Something is significant because of its importance at the time, its depth of impact, or its ____.
The word ____ introduces a final judgement or weighs up the overall argument.

data.title: Steps to build a strong PEEL historical paragraph
items: Make a clear point that answers part of the question
Add accurate evidence to support the point
Explain how the evidence supports the point

data.title: The process from source to supported argument
items: Identify a detail in the source (content)
Make an inference from the detail
Select it as evidence for a historical point
Explain how it supports the point

data.title: Steps to judge the significance of a historical event
items: Choose relevant significance criteria (e.g. number of people affected, long-term impact)
Find evidence that relates to each criterion
Apply the criteria to the event
Compare the event's significance across different criteria
